title: Fever in the returned traveller (adult)
subject: infectious-disease
summary: Exclude malaria first in anyone febrile after travel to an endemic area in the past year, risk-assess for viral haemorrhagic fever if illness began within 21 days of exposure, use itinerary and incubation period to target dengue, enteric fever and rickettsial infection, and admit readily.

sections.title: First steps
items: VHF risk assessment before routine work-up: travel to a VHF area, contact with a VHF case or their body fluids, or laboratory work with VHF agents within 21 days before onset. A substantial proportion of VHF patients have no fever at presentation, so assess anyone with an acute illness and a history of feverishness (UK ACDP).

Possible VHF: isolate at once in a single side room, keep staff numbers minimal, use the enhanced PPE required locally, and call the infection specialist and public health team before further testing.
Respiratory high-consequence infections (MERS after camel or healthcare contact in the Arabian Peninsula within 14 days, avian influenza, clade I mpox): isolate with airborne precautions.

Urgent malaria test for anyone febrile after travel to a malaria area in the past year: thick and thin films or rapid antigen test with a same-day result. Do not delay malaria testing for the VHF assessment.
Negative malaria test but suspicion persists: repeat every 12 to 24 hours for a total of 3 tests (CDC).
Assess for sepsis (vital signs, lactate) and take blood cultures before any antibiotic.

sections.title: History and incubation period
items: Itinerary at sub-national level with dates, accommodation, activities (freshwater, animals, insect or tick bites, sex, healthcare abroad), malaria chemoprophylaxis adherence and vaccinations. Over 90% of US residents with travel-associated malaria had not adhered to recommended chemoprophylaxis.

Onset under 14 days after exposure: dengue (4 to 8 days), chikungunya (2 to 4 days), influenza, COVID-19, leptospirosis (7 to 12 days), spotted fever rickettsioses, enteric fever (7 to 18 days), falciparum malaria (6 to 30 days).
14 days to 6 weeks: falciparum malaria, hepatitis A and E, acute schistosomiasis (4 to 8 weeks after freshwater exposure), amoebic liver abscess.
Over 6 weeks: vivax or ovale malaria, TB, visceral leishmaniasis, hepatitis B, HIV.

Clues: eschar (African tick bite fever, scrub typhus), petechial or purpuric rash (meningococcus, rickettsia, VHF), jaundice (malaria, leptospirosis, hepatitis), bleeding (VHF, leptospirosis, meningococcaemia), eosinophilia (helminths).

sections.title: Investigations
items: CBC with differential, creatinine, electrolytes, liver tests, glucose, coagulation screen, CRP and urinalysis. Leucopenia and thrombocytopenia suggest dengue, malaria or rickettsial infection.
Malaria films or rapid test (repeat as above), blood cultures x 2 (enteric fever, sepsis), dengue NS1 or RT-PCR with IgM.
Store acute serum for paired serology (rickettsia, leptospirosis, arboviruses).
HIV test for febrile returned travellers (acute HIV); chest X-ray; respiratory multiplex PCR if respiratory symptoms; stool culture if diarrhoea.
A specific cause is found in only about 75%; ask an infectious diseases specialist when the diagnosis is unclear.

sections.title: Malaria
items: Falciparum malaria is a medical emergency. Severe features: impaired consciousness, prostration, seizures, haemoglobin below 7 g/dL, acute kidney injury, pulmonary oedema or ARDS, shock, acidosis, jaundice, bleeding or DIC, hypoglycaemia, or parasitaemia 5% or more.

Severe malaria (any species): artesunate 2.4 mg/kg IV at 0, 12 and 24 hours, then oral follow-on treatment once parasitaemia is 1% or less and oral intake is possible; manage in HDU or ICU (see Malaria protocol).

Uncomplicated falciparum: admit. Artemether-lumefantrine 4 tablets (20/120 mg each) per dose with fatty food: first dose, second dose 8 hours later, then twice daily. CDC (August 2026) extended the course from 3 to 5 days (10 doses) for P. falciparum; check local guidance.
Alternative for uncomplicated falciparum: atovaquone-proguanil 4 adult tablets (250/100 mg each) once daily for 3 days with fatty food.

Vivax or ovale: chloroquine 600 mg base, then 300 mg base at 6, 24 and 48 hours (or an artemisinin combination), then primaquine 30 mg base daily for 14 days or tafenoquine 300 mg single dose once G6PD activity is confirmed normal.
Presumptive antimalarial treatment without a test is rarely justified; reserve it for a severely ill patient from an endemic area when testing cannot be done promptly.

sections.title: Other treatable causes
items: Suspected enteric fever after blood cultures: fluoroquinolone resistance is usual in South Asia, so use ceftriaxone 2 g IV once daily or azithromycin 1 g orally once daily.
Travel to Pakistan (XDR typhoid risk): azithromycin for uncomplicated illness; a carbapenem (meropenem 1 g IV 8-hourly) for complicated illness (see Enteric fever protocol).
Eschar, rash after tick exposure, scrub typhus risk (South or Southeast Asia) or suspected leptospirosis: doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily without waiting for serology.
Dengue: supportive care with paracetamol and fluids; avoid NSAIDs and aspirin; watch for warning signs (see Dengue protocol).

Seriously ill without a diagnosis: after cultures and malaria testing, give empirical IV ceftriaxone, adding doxycycline where rickettsial infection or leptospirosis is possible; use meningitis dosing if there is meningism (see Acute bacterial meningitis protocol).

sections.title: When to admit
items: Keep a low threshold for admitting undiagnosed systemic febrile illness.

Admit: any P. falciparum infection, severe malaria, respiratory distress, haemodynamic instability, altered mental state, bleeding, jaundice, acute kidney injury, dengue with warning signs, suspected enteric fever unable to take oral treatment, or unreliable follow-up.
Possible VHF: manage in isolation and transfer to a specialist unit as directed by the infection and public health teams.
If discharged: a negative malaria result first, a written safety net, and review within 24 hours with repeat malaria testing if fever continues.
Notify public health authorities of notifiable diseases (malaria, enteric fever, dengue, VHF and others as local law requires).

sections.title: Special groups and India
items: Travellers visiting friends and relatives carry the highest malaria risk and often take no prophylaxis; prior residence in an endemic country does not protect.
Pregnancy: malaria is more often severe; seek specialist advice early. Primaquine and tafenoquine are contraindicated in pregnancy. Ask about Zika exposure.
Asplenia or immunosuppression: higher risk of severe malaria and sepsis; lower the admission threshold.

India: many returned travellers are migrant workers or pilgrims returning from sub-Saharan Africa or the Gulf. Consider locally endemic dengue, scrub typhus, leptospirosis, malaria and enteric fever alongside imported infections; Indian NCVBDC malaria regimens for locally acquired infection differ from CDC regimens.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Excluding malaria on a single negative film, or because the traveller took prophylaxis.
Labelling fever as flu or a urinary infection without a malaria test.
Forgetting the VHF risk assessment, or delaying malaria testing because of it.
Treating enteric fever from South Asia with ciprofloxacin.
Giving NSAIDs before dengue is excluded.
Omitting an HIV test in a febrile traveller with rash, pharyngitis or lymphadenopathy.

drugs.name: Artesunate
drugs.notes: Severe malaria of any species; complete with a full oral course once parasitaemia is 1% or less.

drugs.name: Artemether-lumefantrine
drugs.dose: 4 tablets (20/120 mg each) per dose: 0 and 8 hours, then twice daily; CDC now 5 days (10 doses) for P. falciparum
drugs.notes: Take with fatty food. The 3-day course remains in many national guidelines.

drugs.name: Atovaquone-proguanil
drugs.dose: 4 adult tablets (250/100 mg each) orally once daily for 3 days
drugs.notes: Uncomplicated falciparum; take with fatty food.

drugs.name: Chloroquine
drugs.dose: 600 mg base, then 300 mg base at 6, 24 and 48 hours
drugs.notes: Vivax or ovale from chloroquine-sensitive areas.

drugs.name: Primaquine
drugs.dose: 30 mg base orally daily for 14 days
drugs.notes: Radical cure of vivax or ovale; check G6PD; not in pregnancy.

drugs.name: Ceftriaxone
drugs.notes: Suspected enteric fever or sepsis; meningitis needs meningitis dosing.

drugs.name: Azithromycin
drugs.notes: Uncomplicated enteric fever, including XDR typhoid from Pakistan.

drugs.name: Meropenem
drugs.notes: Complicated XDR typhoid; adjust for renal function.
